proposition: The fort counts of the Rigveda are formulaic quantities drawn from a small stock of culturally salient numbers, not an enumeration of a remembered number of strongholds.
rests_on_claims: PUR4J-002; PUR4J-003; PUR4J-006; PUR4J-007; PUR4J-008; PUR4J-009
evidence_for: Four diagnostic predictions for an ENUMERATION reading. Two fail decisively, one holds, and one is INCONCLUSIVE. (1) INCONCLUSIVE — an enumeration should be stable per opponent. Sambara's forts are 99 in three passages (RV 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 7.99.5) and 100 in two (RV 2.14.6, 6.31.4), with the ordinal hundredth completing the 99 at 4.26.3. That is nearly stable, and because PUR4J-008 argues the 99 and the hundredth are ONE schema, '99 and 100' may be one value expressed two ways. This prediction was first recorded as FAILING decisively, on a claim that all of 90, 99, 100, the hundredth and hundreds attach to Sambara; three of those five were wrong. See PUR4J-007 and BF-014. (2) FAILS — an enumeration should not migrate to another class of object. The identical nava-plus-navati- expression counts ninety-nine RIVERS at RV 10.104.8 (PUR4J-006). (3) FAILS — an enumeration should not be systematically completed by a round number. Two of the six ninety-nine passages append 'the hundredth' (PUR4J-008), so 99 functions as one-short-of-a-hundred. (4) FAILS — an enumeration should occasionally produce an irregular figure. Every count is 7, 90, 99 or 100, across 21 passages, ten books and every Arnold stratum (PUR4J-009).
evidence_against: Two things cut against the formula reading and both are here rather than in a footnote. First, the numbers are not freely interchangeable ornament: they sort by narrative cycle (PUR4J-010). Seven forts go with Purukutsa and the Puru in all four of their passages, in wording near-verbatim at RV 1.174.2b and 6.20.10c; 99 and 100 go with Divodasa, Atithigva and Sambara. Ornament should not sort by story. Second, and added on review, the strongest of the four diagnostics does not survive re-derivation: Sambara's forts are 99 three times and 100 twice, which is compatible with an enumeration that rounds. The support for this reading is therefore two clear diagnostics of four, not three, and the strongest one is gone.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish that no fortification underlies any passage, and it must not be read that way. A formulaic count can be attached to a real siege; the number being conventional says nothing about whether anything was besieged. It also does not establish that the counts are late, invented, or purely literary. Constitution section 4J puts 'poetic formula' and 'textual stronghold' in a five-way typology precisely because a passage can be assessed on both axes, and the typology is assigned per passage in 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-typology.csv - never inherited from this row. It also no longer establishes that the count is UNSTABLE per opponent, which was its headline evidence. On the corrected figures the one opponent named often enough to test carries two adjacent values, and that is as consistent with an enumeration rounded to a hundred as with a formula.
falsifier: A passage stating an irregular count of forts (say 23, or 41) would break PUR4J-009 and weaken the whole reading. A second corpus-external attestation of a specific fort count tied to a specific place would move the question out of the text. Demonstrating that nava-navati- at RV 10.104.8 is a scribal or editorial intrusion would remove the migration evidence, though not the Sambara instability. Conversely, finding that the ninety-nine passages share a single poet lineage would strengthen the formula reading by localising it.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv and rigveda-pur-4j-claims.csv PUR4J-002 to PUR4J-010; texts at RV 1.130.7, 2.14.6, 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 6.31.4, 7.99.5, 10.104.8
notes: PROVISIONAL, not VERIFIED: the underlying counts are verified measurements, but the step from them to 'formulaic' is a reading. Held at PROVISIONAL rather than promoted, because the reading is CONVENIENT - it is the deflationary answer, it flatters a sceptical posture, and it costs nothing to assert. proposition: The prominence of ninety-nine in modern citation of the Rigvedic forts is a fact about reception, not a property of the corpus.
evidence_for: Ninety-nine is the second most frequent fort count in the corpus (6 passages against 8 for one hundred, PUR4J-003), it is not the largest, and it is not expressed by a numeral of its own (PUR4J-004). Nothing in the distribution singles it out. It is nevertheless the figure that titles the inherited RV-01 specification, the the-forts page headline, and Version 12 lines 1114, 1164, 1169, 1175 and 1272.
evidence_against: Ninety-nine is a genuinely distinctive expression in a way that one hundred is not: 100 is the ordinary Vedic 'very many' and occurs 14 times in these passages in all functions, while nava-navati- is marked and memorable. Griffith's rendering 'nine-and-ninety castles' is a striking English phrase and is the wording most likely to have carried the number into anglophone circulation. So the salience is not arbitrary - it is a property of the expression, not of the count.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish where MelaKeela's ninety-nine came from. No source is recorded for the the-forts headline anywhere in this repository, and the curatorial audit rates it Medium risk, 'thin or undetected bibliography', 'Revise before release'. The transmission path proposed here - through Griffith's English - is untested and no retrieval was attempted against it.
falsifier: A document showing that MelaKeela's ninety-nine was derived from a corpus operation rather than from the text's numerals would overturn 06-BRIEFS/rv01-reconciliation.md section 2.6 and this row with it. A pre-Griffith English source giving the number would move the proposed transmission path.
notes: The prestige-bias test cuts both ways here and both were run. Demoting 99 because it arrives in a page headline rather than a commit hash would be the error the reconciliation brief warned against; 99 is now a VERIFIED count of six passages, with locators, and outranks the register's 106 on the question of how many forts a passage names. What is demoted is only its claim to be THE number, and that demotion is a measurement.

proposition: The Rigvedic pur- corpus does not describe a single kind of object, and no single English word or archaeological referent can stand for it.
rests_on_claims: PUR4J-013; PUR4J-020; PUR4J-021; PUR4J-022; PUR4J-025; PUR4J-027
evidence_for: Five independent measurements converge. (1) Case: 67.5 percent of simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6 percent locative — the pur is overwhelmingly a thing broken, almost never a place anyone is in. (2) Typology: 47 of 103 passages are figurative and 3 more are both, so very nearly half the corpus is not describing a fort at all — 27 of them divine epithets, lexical (puramdara-) or analytic (puram bhindur). On the rules alone, without any hand override, it is 47 figurative to 54 narrative. (3) Material: 8 of the 10 passages stating a material are figurative or unclassifiable on the hand classification, and 4 of 10 on the rules alone (PUR4J-027); in two of them, untouched by any override, the pur IS a god or a river. (4) Descriptors: one pur is carisnu- 'moving' (RV 8.1.28) and one is ama- 'raw, unbaked' (RV 2.35.6). (5) Lexicography: Grassmann defines the word as an earthwork — 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' — and no translator in the corpus renders it 'city' more than once in 103 passages.
evidence_against: The corpus is not uniformly figurative either, and this is the half that a deflationary reading drops. 48 of 103 passages present a fort as an object in the narrative, 54 on the rules alone; all six ninety-nine passages and all four seven-fort passages are among them; the forts have named holders (Sambara, Pipru, Vangrda, Varcin), stated materials in two enemy cases (stone at RV 4.30.20, metal at RV 2.20.8), a gate (RV 6.18.5), and possibly a proper name (RV 1.149.3, disputed). Whatever else the corpus is doing, it is also describing things that were held and broken.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does NOT establish what a pur was, whether any corresponded to a built structure, or where any stood. It bears on the FORM of the answer — that the answer will be plural — not on its content. Specifically it does not license the inverse error of concluding that no Rigvedic pur was a real fortification: 48 passages present one as an object, and this unit has no evidence bearing on whether any of them stood anywhere.
falsifier: A demonstration that the figurative passages are chronologically or dialectally separable from the narrative ones would replace this with a two-stage account rather than a plural one. A retrieved archaeological or geographic argument tied to a specific passage would move the three unassigned types out of NOT ASSIGNED for that passage and change what the corpus can be asked. Settling the ayas- crux (PUR4J-023) would sharpen point 3 considerably.
